title: How products make money
summary: Learn the few ways products earn money, and how to tell if each order or user makes or loses money.

lessons.title: The main ways to make money
teach: Most products earn money in one of a few ways: selling things, taking a cut (commission), subscriptions, ads, or fees.
Many big products mix two or more. Zomato takes a commission from restaurants, charges delivery fees, and sells ads to restaurants.
The way a product makes money shapes what it builds. Ad products want your time. Subscription products want you to stay every month.

questions.prompt: Match each product to its main way of making money.
questions.explain: Four common models: subscription, ads, commission and direct sales.

questions.prompt: Which is a commission model?
options: Spotify Premium at a fixed monthly price
Uber keeping part of each ride fare
questions.explain: Uber keeps a share of every fare and passes the rest to the driver. That share is its commission.

questions.prompt: A free app can still make a lot of money.
questions.explain: Free apps like YouTube and Instagram earn from ads. Others like Candy Crush earn from a few users buying extras.

questions.prompt: One line gets the money model wrong. Which one?
lines: Zerodha: small fee on each trade
LinkedIn: ads, premium plans and recruiter tools
Canva: free plan plus paid Pro plans
questions.explain: Wikipedia runs on donations and shows no ads. That's part of why people trust it.

questions.prompt: What is 'freemium'?
options: A basic version is free and you pay for extra features
You pay first and get a refund
questions.explain: Notion, Canva and Spotify all give a free version so many people try it, then some pay for more.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 ways Zomato makes money.
options: Commission from restaurants on each order
Delivery and platform fees from customers
Ads that restaurants buy to show up higher
Charging restaurants rent for kitchens they own
questions.explain: Commission, customer fees and ads. Selling personal data would break trust and the law.

questions.prompt: An ad business wants users to spend more time in the app.
questions.explain: More time means more ads shown. That's why Instagram added Reels and endless feeds.

lessons.title: Price and value
teach: People pay when the value they get feels bigger than the price. Price is not about your cost, it is about the value to the user.
Products often use tiers, like Free, Pro and Team, so different people can pay different amounts for different value.
Small changes in price can change who buys. Always watch what happens to sign ups and cancellations after a price change.

questions.prompt: Why does Spotify offer Student, Individual and Family plans?
options: Different people value it differently and can pay different amounts
questions.explain: Students have less money, families share. Tiers let Spotify earn from all of them instead of losing some.

questions.prompt: The right price is always your cost plus a little profit.
questions.explain: Price follows value. Software costs almost nothing per extra user, but Figma charges based on what teams get from it.

questions.prompt: Put these Notion style plans from cheapest to most expensive.
steps: Enterprise with security and admin tools
questions.explain: Each tier adds value for a bigger, richer customer, so the price climbs.

questions.prompt: A food app raises its delivery fee. What should the PM watch first?
options: Orders per user and cart drop off
questions.explain: If people order less or quit at checkout, the extra fee may cost more than it earns.

questions.prompt: Which pricing idea is likely to backfire?
lines: Showing all fees clearly on the cart page
A free trial with a reminder before it ends
Adding a surprise fee on the last screen
questions.explain: Surprise fees break trust and raise drop offs. Quick commerce apps have faced complaints and penalties for this.

questions.prompt: Match the pricing trick to its purpose.

pairs.right: Let people feel the value first

questions.explain: Each trick solves a specific goal: trying, staying, spending more, or reaching new people.

questions.prompt: Swiggy One and Zomato Gold are ways to make users order more often.
questions.explain: Members paid upfront, so they feel they should use the free deliveries. That builds a habit.

lessons.title: Unit economics: money per order
teach: Unit economics means: on one order, ride or user, do you make or lose money? It is the simplest test of a healthy business.
For an order: what you earn (commission, fees, ads) minus what it costs (delivery, discounts, payment fees, support).
A company can grow fast and still lose money on every order. Growth then makes losses bigger, not smaller.

questions.prompt: A delivery app earns ₹60 per order and spends ₹75 per order. What is true?
questions.explain: 60 minus 75 is minus 15. More orders like this mean more losses, until costs fall or earnings rise.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 things that add to what a quick delivery app earns per order.
questions.explain: Margin, ads and fees bring money in. Rider pay and discounts are costs that take money out.

questions.prompt: If you lose money per order, growing faster always fixes it.
questions.explain: Only if growth lowers the cost per order, for example busier stores and riders. Otherwise you just lose more.

questions.prompt: Put the steps to check unit economics in order.
steps: Pick the unit, like one order
Add up what you earn per unit
Add up what each unit costs
Subtract to see profit or loss per unit
questions.explain: Unit first, then money in, money out, and the difference.

questions.prompt: What is 'average order value' (AOV)?
options: How much users like an order
The average amount spent per order
The number of orders per day
questions.explain: Higher AOV helps because fixed costs like the rider trip get spread over a bigger order. That's why apps push 'add ₹50 more for free delivery'.

questions.prompt: One of these will not improve money per order. Which?
lines: Shorter rider trips from closer stores
questions.explain: Bigger discounts cost more on every order. The others raise earnings or cut costs.

questions.prompt: Why do quick commerce apps sell ads to brands?
options: Ads cost almost nothing to add and boost money per order
questions.explain: Brands pay to be seen on the app. That money has almost no extra cost, so it improves profit per order a lot.

lessons.title: Getting and keeping customers
teach: CAC is how much it costs to get one new customer. LTV is how much money a customer brings over their whole time with you.
A healthy product earns much more from a customer than it spends to get them. A common rule is LTV at least 3 times CAC.
Keeping users is cheaper than finding new ones. That's why retention matters so much for money.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Cost to get one new customer
Money a customer brings over time
Time to earn back the cost of a customer

questions.explain: These four numbers tell you if growth is healthy or just expensive.

questions.prompt: An app spends ₹500 to get a user who brings ₹300 in total. What should it do?
options: Fix it: lower CAC or raise LTV
questions.explain: It loses ₹200 per user. Spending more just loses more. Make users stay longer or find cheaper ways to get them.

questions.prompt: If fewer users leave each month, LTV goes up.
questions.explain: Users who stay longer pay for longer. Netflix works hard on retention for this reason.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 things that raise LTV.
options: Higher margin on what they buy
More money spent on TV ads
questions.explain: LTV is roughly time stayed x spend x margin. Ads and offices change costs, not the value of a user.

questions.prompt: One of these is not a cheap way to get users. Which?
lines: Big celebrity TV ads every week
questions.explain: TV ads with celebrities cost a lot per user. Referrals, search and word of mouth are usually much cheaper.

questions.prompt: Why do apps like CRED and PhonePe give cashback?
options: To get and keep users, hoping they earn more from them later
To lose money on purpose forever
questions.explain: Cashback is a CAC and retention cost. It only works if those users later bring in more money, for example through loans or ads.

questions.prompt: Order these from what you check first to last when growth feels too costly.
steps: Look at how many users stay after 30 days
Compare LTV to CAC and cut bad channels
questions.explain: Know what you spend, see who stays, estimate value, then decide.
